wa_liberty_bell_freedom_or_death.beta: P1 (5.10b/c) climbs a face-and-crack system to bolts on a slab, needing 4-5 gear placements before the first bolt. P2 (5.11c) steps left off the anchor, following rightward-trending bolts with room for a finger-sized piece. P3 (5.12a) follows bolts up and left through sustained, hard-to-aid climbing (bring a .5, .75 and #1 Camalot). P4 (5.10c) is an awkward, rough traverse left rejoining Liberty Crack, rated 11+R on the topo but reported as feeling more like PG13.

wa_up_in_arms.beta: Six sustained pitches of corners and cracks (with a bit of aid still occasionally used by the first ascensionists) up a sunny, southwest-facing wall; the hardest climbing is on pitch one. Three fixed protection bolts and one bolted anchor supplement gear. The route earned a 3-star rating in its first documented ascents.

wa_golden_age.descent_text: Because belays aren't uniformly bolted for rappel, most parties descend by walking off or by joining the Tiger's or Ellen Pea's rappel line rather than reversing Golden Age directly.
wa_golden_age.rappels: Not all belays are bolted for rappel; most parties walk off or join the Tiger/Ellen Pea rappel line
wa_golden_age.beta: A sinuous line up the upper wall with bolted belays throughout (though not all are rappel-ready); rock quality varies, with the crux 4th pitch offering the best stone on the route.
wa_golden_age.approach: Reach the base by climbing the early pitches of either The Tiger or Ellen Pea to the shared midway ledge system, then traverse left to the start; a two-bolt anchor sits on the ledge below the trees.

wa_spontaneous_distraction.rappels: Rappel the route; one 70m rope is sufficient
wa_spontaneous_distraction.descent_text: Descend by rappelling the route itself using a single 70m rope; alternatively, parties finishing higher on the peak can rappel down from Spontaneity Arête's descent line to reach the gully near this route.

wa_castle_in_the_sky.descent_text: From the west summit, descend via the south-side snow slope and ridge scramble back toward Perfect Pass, as on the South Spur route. In an emergency, the upper corner systems (pitches 2-6) could be downclimbed or rappelled off gear anchors, but this was not the descent used on the first ascent.

wa_fortune_peak_standard_route.approach: From the Esmeralda Trailhead (#1394, 4,269 ft), hike the Esmeralda Basin Trail (shared with the Lake Ingalls/Ingalls Way trail for the first 0.4 mi), then continue on the Ingalls Way trail toward Lake Ann. At the trail junction below the pass, head up toward Lake Ann and the saddle above it, then leave maintained trail and follow the ridge boot path to the summit.
wa_fortune_peak_standard_route.beta: Hike the Esmeralda Basin Trail to its junction with the Ingalls Way/Lake Ann trail, continue toward Lake Ann up to the pass/saddle above the lake, then leave the trail and follow an established climbers' boot path along the ridge to the summit.
wa_fortune_peak_standard_route.overview: A straightforward off-trail scramble up Fortune Peak's ridge from the pass above Lake Ann, reached via the Esmeralda Basin and Ingalls Way trails; considered the peak's easiest and most commonly climbed line.
wa_fortune_peak_standard_route.descent_text: The drop from the summit ridge back down to the pass above Lake Ann is steep and, especially early in the season, can remain snow-covered well into summer — downclimb carefully or glissade only after checking the runout. Below the pass, rejoin the maintained Ingalls Way/Esmeralda Basin Trail for the hike back to the Esmeralda Trailhead.

wa_klawatti_peak_sw_buttress.approach: From Seattle, drive I-5 north and then WA-20 (North Cascades Highway) east through Sedro-Woolley, Concrete, and Rockport to Marblemount, then follow Cascade River Road south for about 20 miles — paved for the first 10 miles, gravel and washboard the rest of the way — to the Eldorado parking area near mile 20. From the trailhead, hikers backtrack a short distance along the road to find a safe crossing of the Cascade River (historically a large log or braided ford, which shifts year to year), then pick up a steep, unmaintained climbers' boot path that gains roughly 3,000-3,500 feet through old-growth forest to a boulder field, crosses Eldorado Creek, and opens into the alpine meadows of the Eldorado Creek basin, a common camp area roughly 5-6 hours from the car. From camp, the route continues onto glaciated terrain (roped travel and crevasse-rescue gear required) climbing the Eldorado Glacier to the high camp on the Eldorado-Inspiration ice cap, typically another 3-5 hours. Any overnight stay requires a North Cascades National Park backcountry permit — Eldorado is managed as a high-use cross-country zone with advance reservations available on Recreation.gov plus a limited walk-up allocation issued in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. IMPORTANT — this route is NOT on Eldorado Peak itself, despite being filed under the same area: from the Eldorado/Inspiration Glacier high camp (~7,600ft), continue traversing the Inspiration Glacier well past Eldorado's summit to Klawatti col; Tepeh Towers are passed along this same glacier traverse, and Austera Peak requires further travel across the Klawatti Glacier (including a short rappel from the col) beyond Klawatti Peak — meaningfully further and more committing than simply topping out on Eldorado.

wa_remmel_mountain_nw_ridge.beta: From a high camp at roughly 7,500 ft on the lower ridge, the route follows a long, stable, lightly-vegetated boulder ridge north of the summit. Two main gendarmes block easy passage; each is climbed at about 5.1-5.2 and then a rappel on the west side regains the ridge crest. The line appears sensible as a route; it sees very little traffic. Parties can bypass the technical sections by staying lower on the west slope, avoiding the vertical sections but missing the ridge's technical interest.
wa_remmel_mountain_nw_ridge.rappels: 2, both on the descent - one off each of the two summit gendarmes, on the ridge's west side, covering roughly 30 m of rappelling in total before scrambling down west-slope talus back to camp. Anchors may have to be built from scratch.
